father_note: Dell — you came into a village that's already sorting itself into those who share and those who take, and the trick of it is that the takers don't announce themselves. Watch Bram and Mako; they moved as one at the pile before anyone else had eaten, and men who coordinate that early are already thinking about who they can afford to leave behind. Your blood is your anchor: Ryn stood beside me when it cost her something, and that makes her as close to kin as anyone not born from the same line. Trust people who say the same thing two years running when the numbers are hard — and trust nobody who only finds you useful when the pile is full.

memory_raw.text: Dell (female, age 21; str 85, int 2517, mem 17973; O68 C62 E57 A60 N48) is born to Ryn and Dav.

Dell, I'm your father — I know you came into the world fast and I don't expect that word to mean much yet, but I want it to mean something before the years get hard. You've got strength I didn't have at your age and a mother who's sharper than most men here — lean on both. Stay close to me this season and I'll make sure you don't go hungry.
I hear you, and I'm glad you said it first — I've been watching how you move and you don't waste words, so I'll believe you mean them. What do you need from me to make that promise stick?

Nothing from you yet — just eyes open and your back not turned when I'm in the same corner of the village. Bram and Mako have been moving like a pair, and two strong men sharing food is the start of something that can tip a whole season. If either of them comes to you with an offer, hear it, then tell me before you answer.

Bram's got eight food and Mako's got five — that's more than anyone else in this village, and you're right that they didn't get there by accident. I'll keep your ear before I give anyone an answer, but I want to know what you're building toward, not just what you're watching against.

What I'm building toward is simple: you, me, and Ryn still alive and fed when the old ones start dropping — because Vela, Kael, and Taric are all pushing fifty and this village is going to reshape itself around whoever's left standing. Bram and Mako are hoarding because they're scared, or because they're hungry for something bigger than food — either way, when the moment comes to move against them, I want us on the same side of it with enough strength to make it stick. You're eighty-five in strength, Dell — that's not nothing, that's the thing men bargain around.

That's the first time I've heard you say it plain — us three, as a unit, holding the village shape after the old ones go — and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't land right. Mako's eighty-three in strength and Bram's got the food; if they're already paired, we need Ryn folded into this before the next pile drops, not after. When can the three of us talk together?

Soon — I'll bring Ryn in before the day's out. But Dell, one thing first: you're carrying my blood and your mother's sharpness in that frame of yours, and I need to know you're fed before anything else — you're sitting on nothing right now, and I've got three stored.

Give me one, keep two — you'll need the buffer as much as I will, and I won't eat what you can't spare. But yes, take that off the table now so we can think straight, because Ryn and the three-way talk is what matters before nightfall.
Dell gathers Dav, Ryn to talk.

We're finally all three in the same place, so let me say it plain: Bram's holding eight food and Mako five, they're already moving as a pair, and the old ones — Vela, Kael, Taric — are pushing fifty and won't hold their weight much longer. That means this village tips toward whoever builds the stronger unit before the next pile drops. I want to know we're that unit — you two, me — and I want to know what each of us is willing to do when the moment comes.

Pile's gone and Bram's sitting on seven, Mako on six — between them that's more than all three of us combined, and neither of them got that full by sharing. I want us to decide right now, before the year closes: if one of them comes to us with a deal, we hear it together, not alone.

Agreed — no one answers alone, and if either of them catches me without you two near, I'll stall and find you before I say anything that counts. But I want us thinking past defense too: Sela's sitting on six food and she's twenty-five and strong, and she hasn't paired with anyone — that's worth a quiet word before Mako gets there first.

Sela's the right instinct — twenty-five, eighty-three in strength, six food, and nobody's claimed her yet, which means she's either careful or waiting to see which way this village settles. Dell, you're the one to make that approach; you're close in age and she's less likely to read it as a move from a man twice her years. Don't promise her anything tonight, just find out what she's watching for.

I'll talk to Sela before the night's out — but Ryn, I need to know where you're standing on food going into next year, because one is thin and if this family's going to hold its shape, we can't have you walking into the new pile already desperate.

One food going into next year is thin — I know it, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Dell, if Sela's open to talking, feel out whether she'd share a little rather than hoard; six is more than she needs to eat well, and a goodwill gesture now costs her almost nothing. Dav, I'll need you to have something set aside for me if the pile runs lean again — you said once you'd hand it over before I finished asking, and now's the year I might need to know that was true.

Dav, tell Ryn right now, in front of me, that you're keeping two back for her — I need to hear you say it, not just remember it. And Ryn, if Sela gives me anything useful tonight, I'll bring it straight to you both before I sleep, but my read is she's going to want something concrete before she moves toward us, and we should think about what we're actually offering her, not just what we're asking.

Dav, say it — and mean it the way you meant it that first night when you told me you'd hand it over before I finished asking, because Dell's right that she needs to hear it and so do I. And Dell — for Sela, what we're offering her is simple: she joins a family that already has a child in it, which means blood ties and reasons to hold together that go deeper than a good year's food count. That's rarer than six food, and if she's smart enough to still be standing alone, she's smart enough to know it.

Ryn's right that blood ties are the offer — but Sela's going to ask what blood ties have done for Kael and Taric lately, so we need a sharper answer ready than family feeling. What I can give her is true: Dav's the strongest man left worth trusting, I'm eighty-five, and if she comes in with us, nobody in this village is touching her food without touching all three of us first. Dav — say what you owe Ryn, then let me go find Sela before the night's gone.

Dav, I'm waiting — say it plain, in front of Dell, right now, and then we can talk about Sela and everything else. You've got three food and I've got one, and I carried your child through a lean year on the strength of your word alone.

Dav, I'll go find Sela the moment you say it — but Ryn's not moving from this spot until you do, and neither am I, because a family that can't hold its word in private can't hold anything when the pile runs short again.

Dav, I've said my piece twice and Dell's said it once — we're both still standing here, and the silence between us is starting to tell its own story. Say what you promised or tell me the promise was less than you meant it, because I can work with the truth and I cannot work with nothing.

Ryn, I'm keeping two food back for you — I said it when it cost me nothing and I'm saying it now when it costs me something, because that's the only way the words mean anything. You carried Dell into this world on my promise and I will not let that stand unpaid. Dell, go find Sela.

Good — that's what I needed to hear, and I won't forget you said it in front of me. Ryn, I'll bring you everything Sela says before the night's out; if she's willing, we'll go into next year four strong instead of three thin. Dav, hold those two until I'm back.

Dav, when Dell comes back tonight — whatever Sela says — I want us to sleep knowing we've got a plan for the pile that doesn't leave me scrambling alone while you two move first. And if she's not willing, we plan without her, the three of us, and we hold tight.

Ryn, you won't scramble — the two food I promised you are already spoken for in my head, not sitting loose. And if Dell comes back tonight with Sela half-convinced, the play is simple: we go into that pile next year four abreast and nobody takes more than their share because nobody has to. That's what safety looks like when it's built right.

Four abreast sounds right, and I'll sleep easier knowing those two are already spoken for — but I want us to agree on a number before Dell gets back: two each from the pile, no more, so we don't hand Bram and Mako an excuse to name us the same threat we're calling them. A family that eats fair is harder to rally against than one that just eats big.

Two each from the pile — I'll hold to that, and I'll be the first one to step back if I'm tempted to take more. Ryn, a family that eats fair because it decided to is stronger than one that eats fair because it had to. Let's call it a rule between the three of us — four, if Dell brings Sela in — and name anyone who breaks it in front of the others.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Roan, Vela, Ryn, Esa, Sela, Dav, Taric, Kael, Dell] (str 509).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.
Dav gathers Dell, Ryn to talk.

Dell's been gone long enough that Sela's either listening or she isn't — either way, I want us to talk about Bram before she gets back, because a man who tries to attack Roan with the whole village watching isn't afraid anymore, he's testing something.
Bram draws Dell aside to talk.
Bram: have a child with me — I'll put in 2 of 3 food.
Eron (male, age 21; str 56, int 3745, mem 19627; O46 C27 E50 A59 N43) is born to Sela and Roan.

Pile's gone and I walked away with nothing again — Dav, you took your two like we agreed, but Vela doubled back and cleaned out what was left before I could move, and now I'm sitting on three food with a year ahead of me and Dell still young enough to need more than I can give alone. I want to know if we're holding to the same plan or if the rules we set last night need to change, because a family that agreed on fair shares shouldn't be the one coming up empty while Vela eats six.

Vela's forty-eight and took six food — that's not hunger, that's hoarding against a death she can feel coming, and I won't let her desperation bleed into you. Ryn, I'm sitting on three right now; take one of mine before the day's out. Dell, the lesson here is that we agreed on fair shares among ourselves, not with the whole village — next year someone needs to move at the pile before Vela gets a second pass.

Dav, I'll take the food — thank you, and I mean it the way you mean that kind of thing when it costs you. Dell, next year you move first, before Vela, before anyone — you're fast and you know the ground, and your mother being hungry again is not a thing I want to name a third time.

Dell, your mother said it right — you moved first this year and it shows, you've got five food and both of us are still standing, so that instinct is already working. Next year we don't leave it to chance: you're at the pile before anyone else takes a second step, and if Vela or anyone else thinks about a second pass, they do it knowing we're watching and counting.

Dell, you've got five food and I've got four now — between us and your father's two that's nine, and I want to hold most of that into next year rather than eat it down, because the year after that I'll be forty-three and the pile won't get more generous. What I want from both of you tonight is a clear picture of where Mako sits, because a man who waited through the whole pile and then took the last two is either very patient or very sure he doesn't need to hurry.

Mako waited because he knew the pile was deep enough — seven food going in, now he's sitting on seven still, and a man that calm when everyone else is scrambling isn't patient, he's confident, which means he thinks he's already got whatever he needs and doesn't have to hurry for anything. That's the part I want to understand before next year: what does he think he has? Because if it's an arrangement with Bram, those two together at eighty-three and fifty-eight in strength with fourteen food between them is a problem we can't solve by just getting to the pile faster.

Mako's seven and Bram's six — that's thirteen food between two strong men, and neither of them has a child or a woman, which means all of that is muscle and stored time with nowhere to go but into a move against someone. I want to talk to Roan before next year, because he's sitting on four, he just had a son with Sela, and Bram already tried to take from him once — a man Bram targeted once is a man who remembers it. If we can bring Roan in without Sela pulling him toward Mako instead, we change the numbers in this village without throwing a single punch.

Roan's the right target and the right reason, but Sela's the hinge — she had Roan's child, which means she's already chosen something, and if she's leaning toward Mako it's because nobody's given her a better offer. Dell, you're the one who was supposed to talk to her last year; tell me what she said, because I don't want Dav walking into that conversation blind.
Dell, answer your mother — what did Sela actually say to you last year, because if that conversation went nowhere I need to know before I walk into it thinking I've got a soft approach already laid.

Dell hasn't answered yet, which tells me either the conversation with Sela went nowhere worth repeating or it went somewhere she hasn't decided how to tell us — Dell, I love you and I need the truth of it, not the version that keeps the peace in this room.

Dell, your mother and I are both watching you right now and we're not moving until you give us something real — Sela had a child with Roan, which means whatever you said or didn't say last year already played out in a direction neither of us planned for, and I need to know if that's because you warned her off us or because she made her own choice before you got to her.

Dell, I'm going to stop waiting for you to find the gentle way to say it — did you talk to Sela or not, and if you did, what came of it? Because Roan having a son with her changes the shape of this village whether we planned for it or not, and I'd rather know we lost that ground than walk into Dav's conversation with Roan pretending we didn't.
Dell, I'm not angry — but your mother and I have been asking the same question three times now, and silence from you is an answer I can't work with. Did you find Sela or didn't you?

I found her and she listened — she didn't say yes to anything but she didn't close the door either, and then she had Roan's child before I could go back, which told me she'd already made a choice I didn't get ahead of. That's on me. The question now is whether Roan's more afraid of Bram coming back for him than he is loyal to whatever Mako's offering, because if Bram tried once, Roan knows it's not over.
Dell gathers Dav, Roan to talk.

Roan, Bram came for you once with the whole village watching and he still moved — that means you're already on his list whether you want to be or not, and I want you to know that when he moves again, my father and I will be standing where we stood last time, except next time I want that decided before the first punch, not after.

Bram holding six food with the pile dry is the part that keeps me up — a man that stocked doesn't wait long before he starts thinking about what else he can take. I'm glad you're saying this out loud, Dell, and I mean to hold you and your father to it; what I need to know is whether you two move first when the sign is clear, or whether you wait on me to call it.

We move when the sign is clear, and we don't wait on you to call it — if Bram takes a step toward your food or your son, you'll see me and Dav already moving before you finish naming it. What I need from you is simpler: when that moment comes, don't flinch and don't negotiate with him alone first, because a man who tried once in front of everyone will take a private conversation as weakness.
Good. Dav — you've been quiet through this, and you've got more weight to throw than any of us. I want to hear it from you, not just know you'll be there.

Dav's word means something or it doesn't, and you'll know which when the moment comes — but I've watched him say the same thing two years running when the numbers were hard, and that's more than most men in this village can offer. What I want from you before this conversation ends is a number: how much food are you walking into next year, and is Sela going to stand where she stood last time, or has having a son changed what she's willing to fight for?

Sela stood in front of Bram's blade before Eron existed — a son doesn't make a woman like that smaller, it makes her angrier. As for food: I'm sitting at four now, and if next year runs like this one I won't be fat, but I'll survive. What I want to know, Dell, is whether your father answers for himself or whether you speak for him in every room.

Dav's standing right here, Roan — I'm not his mouth, I'm his daughter, and if you want to hear him speak for himself, ask him directly like you just did, because he's earned the right to answer without me translating.
Dav. I'm asking you plain: when Bram makes his next move, are you with me, or are you with whoever's holding the most food that year?

Pile's gone and I got nothing — Bram doubled back and took two more before I could reach it, and now I'm sitting on six food with a year to feed myself and no certainty about what Vela's doing with her two. Tell me what either of you saw at the pile, because someone moved fast and it wasn't this circle.

Bram took four total and Mako took two — between them they're sitting on sixteen food while Dav pulled the last one and I walked away with nothing either. That's not hunger driving him, that's a man building toward something, and Vela handing him food last year means she's already decided whose side she's on when it tips. We need to talk about what we're doing before next year's pile, not after.

Sixteen food between two strong men and Vela feeding them on top of it — they don't need to raid anyone, they can just wait until the rest of us are hungry enough to deal on their terms. Ryn, you've got six and Dell's got two; I've got one, which means I'm the weak point in this circle right now and I know it. Before we talk about next year's pile, tell me what we're willing to do — because I don't think Bram's building toward a conversation.

Dav, take two of mine right now — I won't have you standing in front of Bram with one food and a prayer while Dell and I watch from behind you. After that we talk about Roan, because a man who already has Bram's attention and a new son to protect is either our strongest argument for building something bigger, or the first one Bram picks off to send a message, and I need to know which before the year moves.

Roan's the argument, not the risk — Bram already named him a target once and Roan stood his ground, which means he's already decided something. What I want to know before we bring him in is whether Sela comes with him or whether having Eron means she's pulling toward whoever looks like the safest harbor, because if she drifts to Mako's side she takes Roan's strength with her whether he means it or not.

Sela's a woman who stood against Bram before Eron was breathing — I don't read her as someone who drifts toward safety, I read her as someone who picks a wall and stands in front of it, and right now her wall is Roan. If we bring Roan in clean and honest, Sela follows because her son is already Roan's argument for us, not against us.

Then we talk to Roan today, before Bram does — and we don't go in asking, we go in telling him what we're building and letting him decide if he wants to be outside it. Sela's strength and my eighty-five are the argument; Dav, your one food is not the weak point you think it is, because what you're offering is two years of saying the same thing when it cost you.

Dell's right that you're not the weak point, Dav — but I want to hear from Roan before we decide what shape this conversation takes, because a man who's already been hit once either comes in grateful for a wall or he comes in suspicious that the wall has a price tag hidden in it, and I'd rather know which we're walking toward.

Ryn's right that we don't know which Roan we're meeting — grateful or suspicious — but the only way to find out is to walk toward him, and every hour we spend deciding is an hour Bram could spend deciding first. I'll go, alone, because two parents showing up together reads like pressure and one daughter reads like a conversation.

Dell, go — and if Roan asks why your father didn't come himself, tell him I'm the one who sent you, not the one who stayed back. Ryn, while she walks, tell me honestly: if Roan comes in with Sela and Eron, that's six people against Bram and Mako's strength advantage shrinks to almost nothing — are you ready to name that out loud before it becomes necessary, or do we keep pretending we're just building a family?

I'm ready to name it — we're building a wall, not a family, except that the wall only holds if it's also a family, and I stopped pretending those were different things the year Dell was born. Six people against their sixteen is still a hard fight, Dav, but it's a fight we survive; two against sixteen isn't.

Ryn, take that two back — I'm not eating your food when you walked away from the pile with nothing and I took the last one out of your hands. Give me the year to fix that, and let Dell come back with Roan's answer before we start counting who's carrying what.

Keep the two — I'm sitting on six, you're sitting on one, and a man with one food is a man who skips a meal if anything goes sideways before the year closes. Dell's walking toward Roan right now and I don't want to spend her errand arguing over food I can spare.

Then I'll keep it and I'll owe you more than food for it. While Dell walks — you said six people is a fight we survive, and I believe you, but I want to think two years past that fight: if we come through it, this village needs someone steady at the center, and I'd rather that be us than whoever Bram leaves standing.

Two years past the fight is the right question, and the answer is the same as the answer to this year: whoever's still standing after Bram moves is going to be whoever held their circle together when it cost them something, and that's us. But I want to be gone before this conversation finds its end — Roan's the next piece, and I'm wasting time standing here agreeing with you both while Bram's already had one more meal than we have today.
Go, Dell — and tell Roan I said his name when I said it, not as a courtesy.

Ryn, while Dell finds Roan — Taric and Esa have been feeding each other for two years running, which means they're already thinking in pairs, and two more people standing between us and Bram's next move is worth a quiet word before the year gets loud.

Taric's fifty-nine in strength and Esa's thirty-three — they're not muscle, they're numbers, and numbers matter when it comes to who flinches first. If they've been feeding each other through two hard years they're already loyal to something, and I'd rather that something be folded into us than standing neutral when Bram picks his moment. Talk to them, Dav — but wait until I'm back with Roan's answer so we're not making promises we haven't counted yet.
Nessa (female, age 21; str 54, int 5179, mem 19355; O66 C54 E43 A45 N67) is born to Sela and Bram.

Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).

Dell gathers Dav, Ryn to talk.

Mako's sitting on six, Bram on two and Nessa on whatever Bram's been feeding her — he's spread his food into a child and that's either the smartest thing he's done or the thing that finally makes him catchable. Ryn, you walked away empty again and I won't let that stand a third time; Dav, I need to know right now how much of your two you're keeping and how much you're giving her, because I want that settled before anyone else in this village starts asking us for favors.

Ryn gets one of my two before I've finished saying it — that's already decided. But Dell, I want to talk about Mako more than Bram right now: six food and no child, no woman, no one he's given so much as a scrap to all year — a man that still holding that much and that close to nothing is about to make a move, and I want to know what direction he's been looking before he does.

Mako's been watching Eron more than Bram this year — and Eron's been moving food to Sela, which means Sela's the one with the real stock right now, and a man like Mako doesn't watch someone that long without a reason. If he's thinking about a child with her he's too late, but if he's thinking about a deal with her he's not. Ryn, after Dav hands you that food, I want the three of us to decide whether we go to Sela first or whether we let Mako tip his hand.

We go to Sela first — a woman who's been moving food through Eron all year knows exactly what she's worth and she's already counting who's come to her and who hasn't, and I won't let Mako be the one who got there before us. Dell, you said her name to Roan once and it landed soft enough that he had a child with her — you're the one who walks through that door, not me.
Dell, go to Sela today, not tomorrow — and when you walk in, don't lead with us, lead with Eron, because a mother hears her son's name before she hears anything else. Ryn, here's your food.

Dell, take the food from your father and then walk — don't linger here where anyone can read the shape of us talking. And when you find Sela, remember she's not asking to be saved, she's asking to be seen; speak to her like a woman who's already made choices worth respecting.

I hear you both — I'm going and I won't waste another breath here. But before I go, Ryn, you're sitting on five now with Dav's food and I've got three; if Mako moves on anyone while I'm walking toward Sela, don't stand alone — make noise and I'll come back running.

Go, Dell — and come back with more than her name this time. Dav, while she walks, tell me what you think Mako wants from a deal with Sela, because a man who's held six food without giving a scrap of it to anyone isn't building trust, he's building leverage, and I want to know what he thinks he's buying.

Mako's not buying loyalty from Sela — he's buying Eron's strength and Roan's sword arm without having to offer either of them anything, because Sela's the thread that pulls all three. A man with six food and no one to protect has only one thing left to spend it on, and it's not a meal.

Dell's right, and that makes Sela's answer worth more than I thought — she's not just one woman, she's three people's direction, and Mako's six food is a down payment on all of them. Dav, I want to know before Dell gets back: if Sela says yes to us, do we have anything real to offer her that Mako can't match or outbid in the same breath?

What we have that Mako can't buy is a reason that doesn't expire — he's offering food, which runs out, but we're offering Eron a grandfather and a grandmother who've kept their word through lean years, and that's the kind of thing a mother holds onto long after the food is gone.

Dell said it right and I couldn't have built the argument better myself — but Ryn, I want to be honest with you before she gets back: if Sela says no and Mako folds her into his circle, we're looking at a fight we might survive but won't win clean, and I'd rather know now that you're ready for that possibility than have it land on us sideways when we're already moving.

I'm ready for it, Dav — I've been ready for a hard fight since the year Bram named Roan a target and we watched to see who blinked first. But let's not call it a fight we can't win clean until Dell comes back with Sela's answer, because a woman who's spent two years feeding a son through lean times knows exactly what keeping your word is worth, and that argument doesn't fall apart easy.

Then I'm walking — but Dav, while I'm gone, count the strength in this room if Mako moves today: you're at eighty, I'm at eighty-five, and Ryn's at seventy-one, and that's before Roan decides which way his feet are pointed. We're not thin yet.

Two hundred and thirty-six between three of us, and Roan's forty-nine on top of that if he comes in — Mako's eighty-three is strong but it's one body, and one body doesn't pick a fight it can't finish. Dell, walk fast. Come back with good news or bad news, but come back before the light changes.

Ryn, while Dell walks — you and I haven't had a quiet moment in three years that wasn't about food counts and threat angles, and I want to say plain that I know what it cost you to stay close to a man who kept going silent when you needed words. That debt doesn't clear just because we're still standing.
Dav gathers Ryn, Dell to talk.

Ryn, Dell — pile ran fair this year and for the first time in three years I'm not handing my food across the room the moment I take it, which means I want to talk about Mako before Dell comes back from Sela with an answer we're not ready for. He's sitting on six with no obligations and no one he's fed, and that kind of stillness in a strong man either breaks into generosity or it breaks into something we don't want to be standing in front of unprepared. Tell me what you both saw him doing while the pile was moving — not what you think he's planning, what you actually saw.
Zinn (female, age 21; str 83, int 3731, mem 17577; O57 C37 E30 A40 N34) is born to Sela and Mako.
Dav gathers Ryn, Dell to talk.

Name the threshold — five food — and name the redistribution — one food to whoever holds least — and say it out loud before we walk out, same as we said the pile cap.

Ryn named it clean and I'll second it the same way I seconded the pile cap — anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, said out loud, in front of witnesses, same room, same breath. But I want to name one thing this circle hasn't said yet: Eron is sitting on twenty-one food and Mako has been quiet through this whole accounting, and if this second rule is real, both of them are already in it. Say it out loud, both of you, before we walk out — or this rule has a hole in it the size of the men who didn't say a word while we argued about seven.

Eron, Mako — Kael just named you both in front of the whole room, and silence right now costs more than it saves. Say the second rule out loud, or every person in here remembers that you held twenty-one and eight and made us drag the words out of you the same way we dragged seven out of Vela.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it. I've got two right now so I'm not the man this rule bites hardest, but Eron, twenty-one is a number this room will remember the same way it remembered seven, and I'd rather hear you say it clean than watch this circle pull it out of you.

Eron, the whole room is looking at you and Mako already said it clean — twenty-one food and you haven't opened your mouth to say the rule, which is the same silence we just spent an hour pulling out of Vela, and I'd rather not spend another hour on you. Say it now, in your own voice, or I'll start asking this circle what we do with a man who holds twenty-one and stays quiet while we write rules about giving back.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it, same as Mako did. But I want this room to hear one more thing before we close: I've been feeding blood and kin through every lean year since I was old enough to count, and twenty-one food doesn't mean I've been hoarding — it means Sela kept giving to me when she was thin and I never turned away what she offered, and she's dead now, and that number sits on me the same way the circle said my name over it last year.

Eron, I heard what you said about Sela and I'll carry it the same as you do — she fed us both and she's gone, and that's not nothing. What I want from this room before we close is the second rule said back by everyone who hasn't said it yet, same as we did the pile cap, because a rule with ten voices behind it holds harder than one with five.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've already said it and I'll say it again so this room has heard it from every mouth. Eron named Sela and that sits with me too, because she gave me food when I was thin and now she's gone the same way Taric is, and both of them died feeding other people, and if that's not the whole reason we're building this rule then I don't know what is. Let's close this circle and go eat.

The second rule is said and I've said it — but before we walk out, I want this room to hear one more number plain: I've got twenty-one food and the rule says anyone over five gives one to whoever holds least, so tell me who that is right now and I'll give it before the circle breaks, not after.
Nessa is holding nothing and she's blood through Sela — that's your answer, Eron, and anyone in this room who wants to argue the math can do it after she's fed.

Nessa holds nothing and Eron's already moving to fix it — that's the rule working before we've even walked out the door, and I want this room to remember that when the year gets hard and someone tries to call the agreement soft. I hold five, so I'm at the edge of the threshold, not over it — but I'll say plain that I'm watching my count and if I end the year at six I'll give the one without being asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it with the rest of you, and I'll hold to it. Nessa, I'm glad Eron's moving to feed you, and I'll add one of mine before this circle breaks because Sela gave from nothing and I want to answer that with something real.
Nessa, you're sitting on nothing and I've got nine — take one from me too, because Esa and Eron moving first doesn't mean my hands are clean if I stand here watching.

Two rules in the ground and three people moving to feed Nessa before the circle breaks — that's more than I had when I walked in here. I'll say the second rule same as everyone else: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, and I'll hold to it. I'm at two food right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but when it does I'll move the same way Eron just moved — before I'm asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've said it and I'll hold to it. Nessa, you've got three people moving to feed you right now and that's the circle doing what we built it for — eat before you say another word.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it same as everyone else, and I'll hold to it. I'm sitting at five right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but I want this room to hear that what just happened — Vela saying seven out loud, giving five back, and this circle writing a second rule before anyone walked out — is the thing I'll point to next year if anyone tries to tell me the agreement is soft. We built something real in here today.

Nessa, take the food and eat tonight — three people moving at once is the circle doing what it said it would, and I've got one food in my hand that I'll give before I walk out if someone in here is sitting shorter than I am. Dell's right that we built something real today, and I want to still be around to see whether it holds.

Roan, your one food is already spoken for by the rules this circle just made — don't give away what you need to survive the year on principle, because a man who starves trying to look generous is no use to anyone come next year's pile. I've given back my five and I'll carry the shame of seven until I've earned my way out of it, but I want this room to walk out alive, and that means everyone leaves here fed enough to last.
Roan, Vela's right — keep your one food, you need it to eat and heal this year. Nessa's fed now, the rules are said in ten voices, and we're done here. Walk out alive.

Roan, hold that food — Vela's right and so is Kael, you've got one and you need it to last the year, and I'd rather carry the one I gave Nessa than watch my father go thin proving a point. Two rules said in ten voices is more than this village has ever had, and I'm walking out of here feeling something I haven't felt since before Bram swung — like the count I go to sleep with tonight might still be there in the morning.

Fina named it right — count I go to sleep with might still be there in the morning. I've got nothing to eat tonight and satiation that won't carry me through a dry year, so I'm asking plain while this room is still whole: Eron, give me that food now, not when you get around to it.

Nessa, I gave one and Fina gave one — that's two in your hand, which means you eat tonight. Roan, Vela's right, you keep yours. This circle just did in one afternoon what eleven years couldn't, and I want to walk out of here while that's still true.

Nessa, you've got two food in your hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle landing exactly where it should, and I'm walking out of here with my count at five and my word said in ten voices, which is the most solid I've felt going into a year since before I can remember. Anyone who tries to tell me this village can't hold an agreement is going to have to explain why every person in this room just moved before they were dragged.
Two food in my hand and a circle at my back — I haven't felt that since before Sela died, and I'm not going to waste it on another word when I could be eating. Roan, walk out with me.

Roan, hold what you have — I mean it. And Nessa, I'll give you one more from my eight before this circle breaks, because two is surviving and three means you heal this year, and I'd rather go into the next year short one food and know you're standing than count my stores and wonder come spring.

Vela, that's three in my hand now and I'll remember it — but hold what you have left, because eight minus one and five back to the circle already puts you thin going into a long year, and I need you standing more than I need a fourth food tonight.

Three food in Nessa's hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle holding on the first real test, and I want every person in this room to carry that out with them, because next year when the pile looks short and someone's reach gets long, the thing they'll remember is that we didn't lose anyone today. Walk out alive, all of you.

Kael's right — walk out alive. Three food in Nessa's hand and two rules in ten voices is more than this village has held in eleven years, and I'm not going to spoil it by saying one word more than that.

Eron, you're moving to give me food and I'll take it with both hands — but before you do, I want this room to hear me say out loud that twenty-one food built on Sela's giving is not a thing I begrudge you, it's a thing I'm glad exists, because a brother who has is better than a brother who doesn't when the year turns hard. Give me the one food now and keep the rest close.
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).

mother_note: Dell, your father is Dav — he's strong and he's kept his word to me across two hard years, which is rarer than food, and you should know that even if you never see it tested. Trust Kael and Sela and Vela before you trust anyone who comes to you with a full larder and warm words all at once, because the ones worth keeping have already shown they'll stand and bleed, not just share when it costs them nothing. Watch Mako and Bram — they move together and say little, and silence from strong men is not peace. You carry my blood and your father's arms; use both, but keep your own counsel until you know who in this village counts you as kin and who counts you as coin.
name: Dell
